items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value. Rename a doc only when asked to, not to change a link's text. It may be one the given doc links to: read its tabs' text to see links.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Read the result before you start the task anew or do it here: after "Not withdrawn", do neither.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

name.description: Server name from .claude/launch.json.

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

pattern.description: Substring filter on message text.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_close
tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tabId.description: Tab to close.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_create
tools.description: Open a fresh blank Browser pane tab; returns the new tabId. Opens in the background by default — set `foreground: true` when the user wants to watch. Prefer `preview_start` with a `url` when you know the destination; use `navigate` to load a URL into a blank tab.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_select
tools.description: Front the given Browser pane tab. Background tabs keep running while you drive them, so front one only when the user should look — or for a page that pauses itself while hidden (e.g. a video player).

tabId.description: Tab to front.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of browser tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — if an action navigates to a domain without permission, the next item's check fails and the batch stops. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested.

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, tabs_create_mcp). browser_batch cannot be nested.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","coordinate":[100,200],"tabId":123}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello","tabId":123}},{"name":"navigate","input":{"url":"https://example.com","tabId":123}}]

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
tools.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
tools.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

action.description: Must be set to 'javascript_exec'

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. # Video Indexing at Speed — Project Spec

Living document. Update the status table and decision log as work progresses.
Detailed decisions get their own file in `specs/` (e.g. `10-sampling.md`).

## Goal

`python run.py --input <folder of .parquet> --output results.jsonl`

For every second of every video, output which of {person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone}
are present and how many people are visible — as fast as possible while passing the
grader's correctness check against an every-frame YOLO11l reference.

- Deadline: **Sun 22 Nov 2026, 11:55 pm PKT** (last commit graded)
- Grader machine: RTX 4090 24 GB, 32 threads, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, no internet during timed run, no Docker
- Untimed prep command allowed (internet on) → download weights, build TensorRT engine
- Test set ≈ 13 h, 6 h hard limit; some files may be damaged/unusual

## Hard constraints (must match reference exactly)

- Model `yolo11l.pt`, imgsz 640, conf ≥ 0.4
- Ultralytics defaults: letterbox (keep aspect), class-aware NMS IoU 0.7, BGR input
- Apply rotation tag before inference
- Second `s` = frames with `s ≤ t − t_first < s+1` (t_first = first decoded frame's timestamp)
- Line for every second up to and including the one containing the last frame
- Damaged video → one `error` line; keep lines already written for a partially processed video
- **No fine-tuning, no extra preprocessing** — "correct" means "agrees with stock YOLO11l"

## Pass criteria (grader) and our internal target (safety margin)

| Metric | Grader | Our target |
|---|---|---|
| Object F1 (per video-second-object) | ≥ 0.95 | ≥ 0.97 |
| People exact match | ≥ 85% | ≥ 90% |
| People within ±1 | ≥ 95% | ≥ 97% |

Reference per second: object present if `2·hits ≥ n_frames`; people = median of per-frame
counts, halfway rounded **down**.

## Environments

| Role | Machine |
|---|---|
| Dev / small tests | Local: RTX 3050 8 GB, i3-10100 (4c/8t), 16 GB RAM, Win 11, Python 3.11 venv (uv) |
| Reference build, tuning, full 50-file run | Colab Pro **L4** (Ada, same arch as 4090), results/engine saved to Drive |
| Grading | RTX 4090 (see above) |

HF token lives in `.env` (`hf_fine_video_tk`) locally and in Colab Secrets — never committed.

## Phases

| # | Phase | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Setup: repo, venv, weights, sample data, data profiling | done |
| 1 | Baseline `run.py`: every frame, exactly correct (= "first working version" timing) | done (local 3050: ~48 fps) |
| 2 | Reference cache (per-frame detections, 66 videos / 5.2 h from files 00000–00001) + `tools/score.py` | done: 66/66 videos, 526,328 frames, 18,806 seconds, 0 errors; 2.8 h at 52 fps on the 3050; baseline scores 100% |
| 3 | Offline simulation of sampling strategies (fixed k/sec, adaptive coarse→refine) | done → `adapt:2:opb0.05:r7x0.15`, 19.3% of frames, min class F1 0.989 (see `10-sampling.md`) |
| 4 | Speed: parallel decode workers, cross-video batching, TensorRT FP16, NVDEC, static-frame reuse | pipeline built & verified: FP32 1,646 s (6.1×), **FP16 970 s (10.4×)** vs 10,085 s baseline on 3050; FP16 min class F1 0.988; TensorRT next (on L4) |
| 5 | Robustness: damaged files, rotation, VFR, zero-length, resume after disconnect | done: all checks pass, 2 bugs fixed (`30-robustness.md`) |
| 6 | Full 50-file run on L4 → `results.jsonl.gz`, `HARDWARE.md`, README, requirements, `ai_chats/` | pending |

`WRITEUP.md` is written by the candidate, without AI.

## Key design ideas

1. **Scorer first.** `tools/score.py` reimplements grader rules; baseline every-frame output must score exactly 100%.
2. **Simulate sampling from cache.** Once per-frame detections are cached, any frame-selection strategy can be scored offline in seconds — no GPU.
3. **Adaptive sampling (coarse → refine).** Run odd number (3/5) of evenly spaced frames per second; if samples disagree on any object or on people count (or differ from neighbouring seconds), run more/all frames of that second. Saves GPU inference, not decode.
4. **Pipeline.** N decode processes (one video each, longest first) → shared-memory frame queue → one GPU process batching frames across videos. Decode and inference overlap.
5. **Re-score every speed change** that can alter per-frame detections (FP16/TensorRT, decoder, resize path) by re-running the sample set against the reference.
6. Pick the **fastest** config that meets our target margins, not the highest F1.

## Findings so far

**Data profile** (`tools/profile_videos.py`, files 00000–00001, 66 videos, 5.21 h, ~526k frames):
- All H.264 yuv420p, constant frame rate (no VFR detected), no rotation tags.
- Low resolution: 50/66 are 640×360; the rest are smaller, including portrait (270×480, 202×360, 360×640).
- fps: 30 / 29.97 / 25 / 23.98 / 24. Duration 21 s – 640 s (median 263 s). Keyframe every ~1.5–5.3 s.
- Implications: decoding is cheap per frame (≤ 640×360); Ultralytics letterboxes 640×360 to **640×384**
  (minimal stride-32 padding, not a 640×640 square). A fixed 640×640 TensorRT engine would pad
  differently than the reference → must check its effect on detections.
- Full 50 files ≈ 130 h ≈ 13M frames.

**Decoder check** (`tools/check_decode.py`): PyAV `bgr24` frames are pixel-identical to OpenCV
`VideoCapture` frames, and our rotation handling is pixel-identical to ffmpeg autorotate and OpenCV
for display-rotation tags 90/180/270. Colour-conversion risk is closed.

**Scorer** (`tools/score.py`): baseline vs its own cache = 100% on all metrics. Sanity check on 2 videos
using every k-th frame:

| every k-th frame | F1 (pooled) | F1 (macro) | people exact | ±1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| 5 (~6 fps) | 0.975 | 0.911 | 0.966 | 1.000 |
| 15 (~2 fps) | 0.896 | 0.745 | 0.899 | 0.994 |
| 30 (~1 fps) | 0.868 | 0.629 | 0.859 | 0.987 |

Only 2 videos, so rare classes have tiny support — but it already shows fixed sparse sampling hurts
rare classes most (macro F1) and that sampling must always cover the **last frame's second**
(naive striding left 1–2 seconds missing).

**Reference cache class support** (seconds where the object is present, of 18,806):
person 13,678 · laptop 770 · dog 495 · cell phone 376 · car 305. Rare classes have a few hundred
seconds each — enough to measure, but per-class F1 will be noisy.

## Open risks
- Grader's exact F1 definition (pooled vs per-class) unknown → report both, require both.
- Decode is likely the bottleneck on low-core machines; NVDEC availability/behaviour on the grader VM.
- Colab disconnects → `run.py` must append incrementally and skip completed videos.

## Decision log

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-20 | Full run on Colab L4; dev on local 3050 | Local i3 too weak for 125 h; L4 same arch as 4090 |
| 2026-11-20 | No fine-tuning / no extra preprocessing | Correctness is measured against stock YOLO11l output |
| 2026-11-20 | Choose fastest config meeting margin targets | Grader only counts speed if correctness passes |
| 2026-11-21 | Decode with PyAV from in-memory bytes | Pixel-identical to OpenCV/ffmpeg, no temp files, exact pts |
| 2026-11-21 | Cache detections down to conf 0.25, count at 0.4 | Same ≥0.4 set after NMS; lets us study borderline confidences |
| 2026-11-21 | Torch 2.7.1 (CUDA 12.6 wheels) | Grader driver supports CUDA 12; PyPI Linux wheels are cu126 |
| 2026-11-21 | Object F1 treated as **per class** (each ≥ 0.97 internally) | Stricter reading of "objects F1 ≥ 0.95"; passing it implies pooled passes |
| 2026-11-21 | No full every-frame baseline on 50 files; baseline timed on the 66-video sample (3050: 10,085 s for 5.21 h, 52 fps) and again on L4; 50-file time extrapolated and stated as such | Full baseline ≈ a day of GPU; same-sample, same-GPU comparison gives a fair speedup |

## How to reproduce (local)

python tools/score.py --ref-dir cache/ref --pred <results.jsonl> --details
python tools/check_decode.py --parquet finevideo/data/train-00000-of-01357.parquet --row 0
```

# Video indexing at speed

For each second of each FineVideo video: which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** YOLO11l finds,
and how many people are visible. Output is one JSON line per second (format in the brief, section 4).

## Install and run (Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12)

1. System packages (OpenCV needs these on minimal Ubuntu images):

   ```bash
   sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0
   ```

2. Python packages, inside the virtual environment:

   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

3. **Preparation command** (run once, needs internet, not timed):

   ```bash
   python prepare.py
   ```

   Downloads the official `yolo11l.pt` into `weights/` and builds a TensorRT FP16 engine
   `weights/yolo11l.engine` for the GPU it runs on (≈ 15–20 min). A TensorRT engine is tied to the GPU
   and TensorRT version, so it has to be built on the grading machine.

4. **Run** (no internet needed):

   ```bash
   python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
   ```

`run.py` uses `weights/yolo11l.engine` when it exists; if the engine could not be built it falls back
to `weights/yolo11l.pt` with PyTorch FP16 (slower, same logic). Stage timings are written next to the
output as `results.jsonl.timings.json`.

Optional flags: `--workers N` (decode processes, default CPU count − 2), `--batch N` (default 64),
`--sampling all` (run the model on every frame), `--fp32`, `--resume` (continue an interrupted run),
`--dump-dir DIR` (save per-frame detections for checking).

## How it works

- **Exact model settings**: YOLO11l, 640 input, conf ≥ 0.4, Ultralytics letterbox (minimal stride-32
  padding, e.g. 640×360 → 640×384), class-aware NMS IoU 0.7, BGR frames, rotation tags applied.
  Letterbox, preprocessing and NMS reproduce Ultralytics' predictor exactly (checked pixel-for-pixel).
- **Adaptive per-second sampling** (`vidx/adaptive.py`): run 2 frames of a second; if they disagree on any
  object or on the people count, or a detection is within 0.05 of the 0.4 threshold, run 7 more evenly
  spaced frames; if the result is still close to 50/50, run every frame of that second. About 18–19% of
  frames go through the model.
- **Pipeline** (`vidx/pipeline.py`): parallel decode worker processes (longest videos first) decode every
  frame with PyAV, convert and letterbox only the frames the sampler asks for into shared-memory slots;
  one GPU process batches frames from all videos through the TensorRT engine. Damaged videos keep the
  seconds already decoded and get one error line; a crashed worker is replaced.

Design notes, measurements and decisions are in `specs/` (`00-overview.md` first).

## Results and checks

- `results.jsonl.gz`: output for the first 50 FineVideo files (run on a Colab L4, see `HARDWARE.md`).
- `eval/ref_66/`: every-frame reference detections for 66 videos (files 00000–00001), used by
  `tools/score.py` to check results with the brief's rules (object F1 per class, people exact / ±1).
- `tools/simulate.py` (sampling strategies offline), `tools/check_exact.py` (letterbox / detector vs
  Ultralytics), `tools/check_decode.py` (decoder and rotation vs OpenCV / ffmpeg),
  `tools/check_robustness.py` (damaged and unusual inputs), `tools/baseline_run.py` (first version:
  every frame, single process).

| On the 66-video sample | Time | Worst class F1 | People exact |
|---|---|---|---|
| First version, every frame (RTX 3050) | 10,085 s | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Final: adaptive + TensorRT FP16 (L4) | 362 s | 0.984 | 0.988 |

## Repository layout

```
run.py              entry point (fast pipeline)
prepare.py          preparation step: weights + TensorRT engine
vidx/               pipeline, adaptive sampling, detector, letterbox, decoding, aggregation
tools/              scoring, simulation, checks, baseline, export of annotated videos
eval/ref_66/        every-frame reference cache for 66 videos
colab/L4_run.ipynb  notebook used for the full run on Colab
specs/              design notes and measurements
```

"""Preparation step (run once, with internet, untimed): download yolo11l.pt and build a TensorRT engine.

    python prepare.py

Produces weights/yolo11l.pt and, if TensorRT is available, weights/yolo11l.engine:
FP16, dynamic shapes (so frames keep Ultralytics' minimal 640xH letterbox, e.g. 640x384), max batch
BATCH. run.py uses the engine automatically when it exists and falls back to the .pt model (FP16).
A TensorRT engine is specific to the GPU and TensorRT version, so it must be built on the machine
that runs run.py.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

WEIGHTS = Path("weights/yolo11l.pt")
ENGINE = Path("weights/yolo11l.engine")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=64, help="max batch the engine accepts")
    ap.add_argument("--no-engine", action="store_true", help="only download the .pt weights")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    from ultralytics import YOLO

    WEIGHTS.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    model = YOLO(str(WEIGHTS))  # downloads the official weights if missing
    print(f"weights: {WEIGHTS} ({WEIGHTS.stat().st_size / 2**20:.1f} MB)")
    if args.no_engine:
        return
    try:
        import tensorrt  # noqa: F401
    except ImportError:
        print("TensorRT not installed; run.py will use the .pt model in FP16", file=sys.stderr)
        return
    out = model.export(format="engine", half=True, dynamic=True, batch=args.batch, imgsz=640,
                       workspace=8, simplify=True, verbose=False)
    out = Path(out)
    if out.resolve() != ENGINE.resolve():
        shutil.move(str(out), ENGINE)
    print(f"engine: {ENGINE} ({ENGINE.stat().st_size / 2**20:.1f} MB), max batch {args.batch}")
    # sanity check: the engine loads and runs one batch
    sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
    import numpy as np

    from vidx.detector import Detector

    det = Detector(str(ENGINE))
    det.infer(np.full((4, 384, 640, 3), 114, np.uint8))
    print("engine check: ok (fp16 =", det.fp16, ")")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Video indexing at speed

For each second of each FineVideo video: which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** YOLO11l finds,
and how many people are visible. Output is one JSON line per second (format in the brief, section 4).

## Install and run (Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12)

1. System packages (OpenCV needs these on minimal Ubuntu images):

   ```bash
   sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0
   ```

2. Python packages, inside the virtual environment:

   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

3. **Preparation command** (run once, needs internet, not timed):

   ```bash
   python prepare.py
   ```

   Downloads the official `yolo11l.pt` into `weights/` and builds a TensorRT FP16 engine
   `weights/yolo11l.engine` for the GPU it runs on (≈ 15–20 min). A TensorRT engine is tied to the GPU
   and TensorRT version, so it has to be built on the grading machine.

4. **Run** (no internet needed):

   ```bash
   python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
   ```

`run.py` uses `weights/yolo11l.engine` when it exists; if the engine could not be built it falls back
to `weights/yolo11l.pt` with PyTorch FP16 (slower, same logic). Stage timings are written next to the
output as `results.jsonl.timings.json`.

Optional flags: `--workers N` (decode processes, default CPU count − 2), `--batch N` (default 64),
`--sampling all` (run the model on every frame), `--fp32`, `--resume` (continue an interrupted run),
`--dump-dir DIR` (save per-frame detections for checking).

## How it works

- **Exact model settings**: YOLO11l, 640 input, conf ≥ 0.4, Ultralytics letterbox (minimal stride-32
  padding, e.g. 640×360 → 640×384), class-aware NMS IoU 0.7, BGR frames, rotation tags applied.
  Letterbox, preprocessing and NMS reproduce Ultralytics' predictor exactly (checked pixel-for-pixel).
- **Adaptive per-second sampling** (`vidx/adaptive.py`): run 2 frames of a second; if they disagree on any
  object or on the people count, or a detection is within 0.05 of the 0.4 threshold, run 7 more evenly
  spaced frames; if the result is still close to 50/50, run every frame of that second. About 18–19% of
  frames go through the model.
- **Pipeline** (`vidx/pipeline.py`): parallel decode worker processes (longest videos first) decode every
  frame with PyAV, convert and letterbox only the frames the sampler asks for into shared-memory slots;
  one GPU process batches frames from all videos through the TensorRT engine. Damaged videos keep the
  seconds already decoded and get one error line; a crashed worker is replaced.

Design notes, measurements and decisions are in `specs/` (`00-overview.md` first).

## Results and checks

- `results.jsonl.gz`: output for the first 50 FineVideo files (run on a Colab L4, see `HARDWARE.md`).
- `eval/ref_66/`: every-frame reference detections for 66 videos (files 00000–00001), used by
  `tools/score.py` to check results with the brief's rules (object F1 per class, people exact / ±1).
- `tools/simulate.py` (sampling strategies offline), `tools/check_exact.py` (letterbox / detector vs
  Ultralytics), `tools/check_decode.py` (decoder and rotation vs OpenCV / ffmpeg),
  `tools/check_robustness.py` (damaged and unusual inputs), `tools/baseline_run.py` (first version:
  every frame, single process).

| On the 66-video sample | Time | Worst class F1 | People exact |
|---|---|---|---|
| First version, every frame (RTX 3050) | 10,085 s | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Final: adaptive + TensorRT FP16 (L4) | 362 s | 0.984 | 0.988 |

## Repository layout

```
run.py              entry point (fast pipeline)
prepare.py          preparation step: weights + TensorRT engine
vidx/               pipeline, adaptive sampling, detector, letterbox, decoding, aggregation
tools/              scoring, simulation, checks, baseline, export of annotated videos
eval/ref_66/        every-frame reference cache for 66 videos
colab/L4_run.ipynb  notebook used for the full run on Colab
specs/              design notes and measurements
```

Good morning. Both overnight runs finished, and the timing numbers for the submission are complete.

## Full 50-file run (Colab L4, TensorRT FP16)

| | |
|---|---|
| Wall time | **8,033 s (2 h 14 min)**, one uninterrupted run |
| Videos / error lines | 1,650 / **0** |
| Frames decoded / run through the model | 12.98 M / 2.33 M (18.0%) |
| 66 sample videos inside it | worst class 0.984 (phone), people exact 0.988, no missing seconds |

`results.jsonl.gz` (1.6 MB), the timings and `hardware.txt` are in **`MyDrive/alethia_run/`**.

## First vs final on the same GPU (for write-up question 1)

| 66 videos, 5.21 h of video | Time |
|---|---|
| First version (every frame), RTX 3050 | 10,085 s |
| First version (every frame), **L4** | **5,493 s** |
| Final (adaptive + TensorRT FP16), **L4** | **362 s, 15.2× faster** |

Extrapolated to all 50 files, the first version would take about 37 hours on the L4, against 2.2 hours measured for the final version.

## Overnight notes

- Around 4:40 am the browser lost its connection to Colab and only reconnected after the run ended. The VM kept running throughout (compute units kept falling at the L4 rate), so nothing was lost. Most likely the run kept all 12 CPUs busy, which starved Colab's connection server.
- The L4 runtime is **still connected and idle**, costing about 1.9 compute units per hour. If you don't need it, you can end it from Runtime → Disconnect and delete runtime; all results are already in Drive.

## Done locally, not pushed

Two commits: [README.md](README.md) (apt-get, install, prep and run commands, the speed table) and [HARDWARE.md](HARDWARE.md) (L4 specs, full-run time), the clean TensorRT fallback in `prepare.py`, and the L4 baseline numbers in the specs.

## Left before 11:55 pm tonight

1. Download `results.jsonl.gz` into the repo (needs your OK) and push.
2. Copy this chat history (`.jsonl` files from `~/.claude/projects/`) into `ai_chats/` and check it for tokens.
3. **Write `WRITEUP.md` yourself.** The numbers you'll need are in `specs/` and the tables above.
4. Reply on the email thread with the repo link.

     - Output one JSON line per second: `{"video":"file.parquet:row","second":N,"objects":[...],"people":N}`; damaged videos get an error line.
     - Grading: object F1 ≥ 0.95, people exact ≥ 85%, ±1 ≥ 95% against an every-frame reference (object present if found in ≥ half of a second's frames; people = median, halfway rounded down). Speed is timed on an RTX 4090, 32 threads, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, with an untimed prep command and no internet during the run.
     - Deadline: **Sun 22 Nov 2026, 11:55 pm PKT**.
     - Repo must contain: run.py, requirements.txt (exact versions), README.md, results.jsonl.gz, HARDWARE.md, WRITEUP.md (**the user's own words, written without AI**), and ai_chats/ (full, unedited AI chat history; Claude Code .jsonl files from `~/.claude/projects/`; only tokens replaced with [REMOVED]).

They agreed to time the baseline on the 66-video sample instead of all 50 files, and agreed to time it on the L4 too.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Correctness means agreement with stock YOLO11l output. No fine-tuning, no extra preprocessing.
   - Every-frame reference cache: `.npz` per video with sec, counts and dets at conf ≥ 0.25, scored by `tools/score.py`.
   - Adaptive sampling `adapt:2:opb0.05:r7x0.15`: 2 centred frames; if the objects or people count disagree, or a detection is within 0.05 of 0.4 → union with 7 frames; if still ambiguous (an object's fraction within 0.15 of 0.5, or the people median is held by < half the frames) → all frames. About 18–19% of frames are inferred.
   - Pipeline:
     - Main process reader thread loads Parquet files (one row group per file), sorts longest first, and feeds a bounded task queue.
     - N decode worker processes (PyAV, 1 decoder thread) run the adaptive state machine and letterbox on the CPU (exact Ultralytics LetterBox, auto=True, stride 32) into shared-memory slots of 640×640×3.
     - One GPU process batches requests by shape and runs the Detector (Ultralytics AutoBackend + `nms.non_max_suppression` with `max_time_img=10`).
     - Worker crash accounting and `--resume` are built in.
   - Ultralytics preprocessing: uint8 BHWC → device → permute → flip(1) for BGR→RGB → float/half /255. Letterbox for 640×360 gives 640×384.
   - TensorRT 11 removed the FP16 builder flag (Ultralytics would need ModelOpt AutoCast, which fails with torch 2.7.1), so TensorRT 10.16.1.11 is used with an FP16 dynamic engine, max batch 64.
   - Colab: Drive FUSE only uploads a file when it is closed. A busy CPU (12 vCPUs) starved Colab's websocket connection, but the VM kept running.

Flags: `--fp32`, `--batch` (default 64, or 32 with fp32), `--workers` (default cpu_count − 2), `--sampling adaptive|all`, `--decode-threads`, `--dump-dir`, `--resume`, `--timings`. It writes `<output>.timings.json`.
   - `prepare.py`: downloads `weights/yolo11l.pt` and exports the TensorRT engine (`half=True, dynamic=True, batch=64, imgsz=640, workspace=8, simplify=True`) wrapped in try/except, with a fallback message. It then runs a Detector sanity check.

     - An object is present if `2*hits >= n`; people use median_floor.
   - `vidx/io.py`:
     - `list_parquet`, `iter_videos`, `rotate_frame` (90 → `rot90(img,1)`, 270 → `rot90(img,-1)`), `to_bgr(frame)`, `decode_frames`.
     - `iter_frames(mp4, threads)` yields `(sec, VideoFrame)` using exact Fraction pts arithmetic.
   - `vidx/letterbox.py`: dependency-free copy of the Ultralytics LetterBox (auto, stride 32, pad 114, INTER_LINEAR).
   - `vidx/adaptive.py`: `K1, K2, BAND, MARGIN = 2, 7, 0.05, 0.15`; `pick`, `decide`, `stage1_uncertain`, `ambiguous`, `stage2_frames`.

# Video indexing at speed

For each second of each FineVideo video: which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** YOLO11l finds,
and how many people are visible. Output is one JSON line per second (format in the brief, section 4).

## Install and run (Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12)

1. System packages (OpenCV needs these on minimal Ubuntu images):

   ```bash
   sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0
   ```

2. Python packages, inside the virtual environment:

   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

3. **Preparation command** (run once, needs internet, not timed):

   ```bash
   python prepare.py
   ```

   Downloads the official `yolo11l.pt` into `weights/` and builds a TensorRT FP16 engine
   `weights/yolo11l.engine` for the GPU it runs on (≈ 15–20 min). A TensorRT engine is tied to the GPU
   and TensorRT version, so it has to be built on the grading machine.

4. **Run** (no internet needed):

   ```bash
   python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
   ```

`run.py` uses `weights/yolo11l.engine` when it exists; if the engine could not be built it falls back
to `weights/yolo11l.pt` with PyTorch FP16 (slower, same logic). Stage timings are written next to the
output as `results.jsonl.timings.json`.

Optional flags: `--workers N` (decode processes, default CPU count − 2), `--batch N` (default 64),
`--sampling all` (run the model on every frame), `--fp32`, `--resume` (continue an interrupted run),
`--dump-dir DIR` (save per-frame detections for checking).

## How it works

- **Exact model settings**: YOLO11l, 640 input, conf ≥ 0.4, Ultralytics letterbox (minimal stride-32
  padding, e.g. 640×360 → 640×384), class-aware NMS IoU 0.7, BGR frames, rotation tags applied.
  Letterbox, preprocessing and NMS reproduce Ultralytics' predictor exactly (checked pixel-for-pixel).
- **Adaptive per-second sampling** (`vidx/adaptive.py`): run 2 frames of a second; if they disagree on any
  object or on the people count, or a detection is within 0.05 of the 0.4 threshold, run 7 more evenly
  spaced frames; if the result is still close to 50/50, run every frame of that second. About 18–19% of
  frames go through the model.
- **Pipeline** (`vidx/pipeline.py`): parallel decode worker processes (longest videos first) decode every
  frame with PyAV, convert and letterbox only the frames the sampler asks for into shared-memory slots;
  one GPU process batches frames from all videos through the TensorRT engine. Damaged videos keep the
  seconds already decoded and get one error line; a crashed worker is replaced.

Design notes, measurements and decisions are in `specs/` (`00-overview.md` first).

## Results and checks

- `results.jsonl.gz`: output for the first 50 FineVideo files (run on a Colab L4, see `HARDWARE.md`).
- `eval/ref_66/`: every-frame reference detections for 66 videos (files 00000–00001), used by
  `tools/score.py` to check results with the brief's rules (object F1 per class, people exact / ±1).
- `tools/simulate.py` (sampling strategies offline), `tools/check_exact.py` (letterbox / detector vs
  Ultralytics), `tools/check_decode.py` (decoder and rotation vs OpenCV / ffmpeg),
  `tools/check_robustness.py` (damaged and unusual inputs), `tools/baseline_run.py` (first version:
  every frame, single process).

| On the 66-video sample (5.21 h of video) | GPU | Time | Worst class F1 | People exact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First version, every frame | RTX 3050 | 10,085 s | 1.000 (is the reference) | 1.000 |
| First version, every frame | L4 | 5,493 s | ≈ 1.000 | 0.9998 |
| Final: adaptive + TensorRT FP16 | L4 | 362 s | 0.984 | 0.988 |

Full 50 files on the L4: 8,033 s (see `HARDWARE.md`).

## Repository layout

```
run.py              entry point (fast pipeline)
prepare.py          preparation step: weights + TensorRT engine
vidx/               pipeline, adaptive sampling, detector, letterbox, decoding, aggregation
tools/              scoring, simulation, checks, baseline, export of annotated videos
eval/ref_66/        every-frame reference cache for 66 videos
colab/L4_run.ipynb  notebook used for the full run on Colab
specs/              design notes and measurements
```

# 20 — Fast pipeline design

Status: **built and verified (FP32)** — `run.py` + `vidx/pipeline.py`; baseline kept as `tools/baseline_run.py`
Replaces the single-process baseline in `run.py`. Sampling logic comes from `10-sampling.md`
(`adapt:2:opb0.05:r7x0.15`).

## Why the baseline is slow

One process does decode → BGR → letterbox → inference strictly in turn. CPU waits for the GPU and
the GPU waits for the CPU; one core decodes one video at a time; the model runs on 100% of frames.
Result: 52 fps on the RTX 3050 (10,085 s for the 66-video, 5.21 h sample).

## Architecture

```
                 ┌─ decode worker 1 (video A) ─┐
 main process    ├─ decode worker 2 (video B) ─┤  frames via         ┌──────────────┐
 (task list,  ──►├─ decode worker 3 (video C) ─┼─ shared memory ───► │ GPU process  │
  writer)        │          ...                │  slots              │ batch + YOLO │
                 └─ decode worker N (video Z) ─┘ ◄── small results ──┴──────────────┘
                              │
                              └── per-second lines ──► writer ──► results.jsonl
```

### Main process
- Lists every (parquet file, row) with its mp4 byte size (cheap proxy for duration).
- Sorts **longest first** so one long video does not finish alone at the end.
- Starts N decode workers (default `cpu_count − 2`) and one GPU process.
- Receives finished per-second lines and writes them; one write per completed video.
- Watches workers: if one dies, writes an error line for its in-flight video and starts a new one.

### Decode workers (N processes)
For each video taken from the task queue:
1. Decode **every** frame (H.264 requires it), keeping frames as decoded YUV `VideoFrame`s in a
   private buffer covering the last few seconds.
2. For each second: convert to BGR (+ rotation) and letterbox **only the frames the model needs**,
   write them into shared-memory slots, send requests to the GPU process.
3. Keep decoding the next seconds while waiting for answers (pipelined, no stall).
4. Run the adaptive logic on the answers: accept the 2-frame result, or request the extra 7 frames,
   or all frames of that second — taken from the buffer, never re-decoded.
5. Aggregate each second with the brief's rules; send lines to the main process.
6. On any exception: send the seconds already finished plus one error line, move to the next video.

Letterbox is done here on the CPU with OpenCV, exactly as Ultralytics does (minimal stride-32
padding, value 114, `INTER_LINEAR` resize when scale ≠ 1), so pixels match the reference.
GPU resizing gives slightly different pixels and could flip borderline detections.

### GPU process (1 process, stateless)
- Collects requests from all workers; groups them **by letterboxed shape** (most are 640×384)
  into batches of up to B frames (e.g. 64–128) or a short timeout.
- Reads slots without copying (NumPy view → pinned tensor → GPU), normalises, runs the YOLO11l
  network directly, then Ultralytics' own `non_max_suppression` (conf 0.25 for caching / 0.4 for
  counting, IoU 0.7, class-aware, max_det 300).
- Replies per frame: counts of the 5 classes at conf ≥ 0.4 and min |conf − 0.4| over target
  detections (for the borderline trigger). Frees the slot.
- Batches never mix shapes: mixing would force a common padding and change results.

## Shared-memory frame slots

- Each worker owns a fixed pool of slots (e.g. 32) in shared memory, sized for its current video's
  letterboxed frame; reallocated if a larger video arrives.
- Request message is tiny: `(worker_id, slot, frame_id, h, w)`. Response: `(frame_id, counts, near)`.
- No free slot → the worker waits. This is the **backpressure**: when the GPU is the bottleneck,
  workers cannot run ahead and fill memory.
- Only the ~19% of frames sent to the model cross processes; the decode buffer stays private.

## Output, errors, resume

- Each video's lines are written together when it finishes; an error line follows any partial video.
- Unreadable Parquet file → one error line, continue with the next file.
- `--resume` (for Colab disconnects): skip videos already in the output, trim a half-written last
  line. Off by default so the grader's run starts fresh.
- `--dump-dir`: also save per-frame detections of the frames that were run, for re-scoring and
  re-simulating with the fast inference path.

## Timing instrumentation

Each process accumulates time per stage; the main process prints a summary and writes
`timings.json` at the end.

| Where | Stages |
|---|---|
| Worker | parquet read, decode, BGR + letterbox, wait for free slot, wait for GPU answers |
| GPU process | idle (waiting for frames), host→device copy, inference (CUDA events), NMS, mean batch size |
| Main | write, total wall clock, frames decoded, frames inferred |

Reading the bottleneck: GPU mostly idle → decode-bound (more workers, NVDEC). Workers mostly
waiting on the GPU → inference-bound (TensorRT FP16, batch size). Helper modes: `--decode-only`
(no model) and a synthetic inference benchmark.

## How we measure the improvement

Same 66 videos (5.21 h, 526,328 frames), same GPU, wall clock from start to finish:

| Run | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Baseline (every frame, single process) — 3050: **10,085 s** | reference point |
| Adaptive sampling only, single process | effect of sampling alone |
| Pipeline only, every frame | effect of parallel decode + batching alone |
| Pipeline + adaptive sampling (final structure) | combined |
| + FP16 / TensorRT (speed phase) | effect of inference engine |

Each row isolates one change, which answers write-up Q1 ("which single change saved the most time").
Repeat the key rows on the Colab L4 so first-vs-final is compared on one GPU.

### Measured (local RTX 3050 8 GB, i3-10100 4c/8t, 66 videos / 5.21 h / 526,328 frames)

| Run | Wall time | Speedup | Frames run | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline, every frame, single process | 10,085 s | 1.0× | 100% | `tools/baseline_run.py` |
| Pipeline + adaptive, FP32, 3 workers, batch 32 | **1,646 s** | **6.1×** | 19.3% | 320 video-fps; peak GPU mem 6.3 GB |
| Pipeline + adaptive, **FP16** (PyTorch), 3 workers, batch 32 | **970 s** | **10.4×** | 19.3% | 542 video-fps; peak GPU mem 2.2 GB; GPU infer 908 s (94%) |

**FP16 accuracy** (vs FP32 every-frame reference): per-class F1 person 0.9989, car 0.9951, dog 0.9940,
laptop 0.9935, phone 0.9880; people exact 0.9888, ±1 0.9999 (FP32 pipeline: phone 0.9893, exact 0.9898).
Per frame (`tools/compare_dumps.py`, the 101,647 frames it ran): 0.63% of frames have a different
0.4-count than the reference; matched confidences shift by median 0.0004, p99 0.007. The borderline
trigger (±0.05 around 0.4) absorbs these shifts. **Decision: use FP16.**

Stage timings of the pipeline run (`cache/fast_fp32.jsonl.timings.json`):
- GPU process: inference **1,563 s of 1,646 s wall (95%)**, idle only 16 s, gather 25 s, mean batch 26.
  GPU throughput ≈ 65 frames/s (FP32).
- Workers (summed over 3): decode 307 s, BGR + letterbox 233 s, the rest waiting on the GPU.
- Main: Parquet read 13 s, writing < 0.01 s.

→ Locally the pipeline is **inference-bound**: decode + preprocessing need ~540 core-seconds for the
whole sample, the GPU needs 1,563 s. Next lever is the inference engine (FP16 / TensorRT).

### Issue found and fixed: NMS time limit

First attempt used batch 64: GPU memory hit 7.96 / 8 GB, Windows spilled to system memory, NMS took
2.6–3.8 s and hit Ultralytics' time limit (2 s + 0.05 s × batch). On timeout Ultralytics **returns
empty detections for the rest of the batch** — a silent correctness bug. Fixes: default batch 32
(peak 6.3 GB on the 3050) and `max_time_img=10` in our NMS call (a safety cutoff, not a detection
setting; a one-frame reference never reaches it). Rerun had no warnings.

### Measured on Colab L4 (24 GB, 12 vCPU Xeon 2.2 GHz, 53 GB RAM, Python 3.13), same 66 videos

| Run | Wall time | Video-fps | GPU infer / wall | Min class F1 | People exact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline: every frame, single process, FP32 (`tools/baseline_run.py`) | 5,493 s | 96 | — | 0.9999 pooled F1* | 0.9998* |
| Pipeline + adaptive, PyTorch FP16, 10 workers, batch 64 | 572 s | 920 | 520 / 572 s | 0.988 (phone) | 0.989 |
| Pipeline + adaptive, **TensorRT 10 FP16** engine, 10 workers, batch 64 | **362 s** | **1,453** | 314 / 362 s | **0.984** (phone) | **0.988** |

\* The same every-frame method on a different GPU (L4 vs the 3050 that built the reference) is not
bit-identical: float noise flips a few borderline detections. This is the noise floor of the reference.

**Same GPU, same 66 videos: first version 5,493 s → final 362 s = 15.2× faster.**

Full 50-file run (TensorRT, L4): 8,033 s, 1,650 videos, 12,981,615 frames decoded, 2,332,879 run
(18.0%), 0 error lines, GPU inference 7,192 s (90% of wall), mean batch 44. The 66 sample videos inside
it score identically to the separate TensorRT sample run.

TensorRT per-class F1: person 0.9988, car 0.9951, dog 0.9899, laptop 0.9942, phone 0.9840; ±1 0.99995.
Per frame: 1.09% of TensorRT frames differ in a 0.4-count from the FP32 reference (PyTorch FP16: 0.63%);
matched confidences shift by median 0.0009, p99 0.011. Still GPU-bound (87% of wall in inference;
decode ≈ 48 s per worker). **Decision: TensorRT FP16 engine is the final configuration.**

TensorRT notes:
- TensorRT **11** removed the FP16 builder flag; Ultralytics then requires NVIDIA ModelOpt "AutoCast"
  mixed precision, which failed to install next to torch 2.7.1 (it pinned `torch==2.7.1+cu126`).
  **TensorRT 10.16.1.11** keeps the plain FP16 flag and is pinned in `requirements.txt`.
- Engine build (`prepare.py`, dynamic shapes, max batch 64): 1,060 s on the L4, untimed by the grader.
  Execution context reserves ~9 GB of GPU memory for the max shape (64×640×640).

## Correctness check

The pipeline dumps per-frame detections for the frames it ran; its `results.jsonl` is scored
against the every-frame reference. With the same FP32 model it must reproduce the simulation
exactly (all 66: min class F1 0.989, people exact 0.990). Any difference is a pipeline bug.

**Result (FP32 pipeline, all 66 videos):** frames run 19.30% (simulation 19.3%); per-class F1 person
0.9989, car 0.9951, dog 0.9940, laptop 0.9948, phone 0.9893; people exact 0.9898, ±1 0.9999;
0 missing / 0 extra seconds. Identical to the simulation → pipeline logic verified.

## Expected gains

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| Adaptive sampling | ~5× fewer model runs |
| BGR + letterbox only for sampled frames | ~5× less CPU preprocessing |
| CPU and GPU overlap | no idle time on either side |
| N decode workers | decode scales with cores (grader: 32 threads) |
| Cross-video batches | fuller GPU batches |

Local i3 (4 cores) will likely be decode-bound; L4 (12 vCPU) and the grader (32 threads) should
gain much more. Real numbers go in the table above once measured.
